title: Microsoft's Brad Smith Hits Back at Vance as Nadella Medal Exposes H-1B Split
excerpt: Smith says Microsoft hired 9,000 US-born workers last year and notes five of six medalists honoured by Trump — including the H-1B alumnus Nadella — were immigrants, as the PERM suspension of eight firms enters week two without a written notice.
body:
• The Labour Department suspended PERM green-card filings by eight employers — Microsoft, Infosys, TCS, Wipro, HCLTech among them — on October 8; no written notice defining the suspension's scope or duration had been published as of October 13, and none of the companies has been charged.
  • Vice President Vance says Microsoft laid off 6,000 US workers last year while obtaining 6,300 H-1B visas and nearly 3,000 green cards; Microsoft says 80% of its roughly 6,000 H-1B filings were extensions or status changes for existing employees.
  • Microsoft president Brad Smith says the company hired more than 9,000 US-born workers last year, and notes five of the six science and technology medalists President Trump honoured the same day — including CEO Satya Nadella — came to the US as immigrants.
  • A Labour Department rule allows PERM processing to be suspended for up to 180 days during a fraud investigation; employees of the eight firms face green-card timelines frozen in the meantime.

The Trump administration's case against Microsoft's use of foreign-worker programmes has drawn a public rebuttal from the company's president — and Brad Smith chose his ground carefully: the medal ceremony held hours after the crackdown was announced.

Two events, one day

On October 8, the Labour Department suspended permanent labour certification (PERM) filings — the mandatory first step in most employer-sponsored green cards — by eight employers, including Microsoft and the Indian IT majors Infosys, TCS, Wipro and HCLTech. Vice President JD Vance, who heads the administration's fraud task force, announced the move at a White House news conference, saying Microsoft had laid off 6,000 American workers while obtaining 6,300 H-1B visas and almost 3,000 green cards. "You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants," Vance said, adding the suspension would "last as long as it needs to."

https://x.com/JBlunt1018/status/2110818910039928980

That evening, President Trump presented Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella — who himself once held an H-1B visa — with the National Medal of Technology and Innovation at a summit in Washington.

"We should consider the fact that when the president honored six Americans with these technology and science medals, five of the six had come to the United States as immigrants."

— Brad Smith, Microsoft vice chair and president

Microsoft's numbers

Smith, in a Politico interview in Dublin reported by IANS and carried by Hi India, said Microsoft hired more than 9,000 US-born workers last year — "a fact that had been left out of the narrative." In its October 8 statement, the company said that of about 6,000 H-1B applications filed last fiscal year, 80% were to extend or change the status of existing employees, that the rest were already legally in the US and equal to about 1% of its US workforce, and that it pays H-1B staff the same as comparable employees, among the highest wages in H-1B filings. Smith warned against signals that send "the most talented next wave" of engineers to other countries.

What remains unresolved

As GeekWire and immigration lawyers note, the suspension's legal footing is thin so far: no written Labour Department notice setting out scope or duration had appeared by October 13, the governing rule permits a suspension of up to 180 days during a fraud investigation, and none of the eight companies has been charged with anything. India's External Affairs Ministry said last week the US steps "do not advance the shared ambitions of both countries."

For the tens of thousands of Indian professionals whose green cards run through these eight employers, the immediate effect is not a ruling but a freeze: PERM filings stall, and with them the already decades-long queue for Indian-born applicants, the largest group of H-1B holders. Whether the administration publishes a formal notice — and whether any company is actually charged — is the next development to watch.
